title: Hydrodynamic attractors
authors: Tilman Enss, Michal P. Heller, Alexandre Serantes, Clemens Werthmann
abstract: Attractors are effective low-dimensional structures, defined in a chosen set of observables, that trajectories from different initial states approach; hydrodynamic attractors are those on which the late-time evolution is governed by hydrodynamic constitutive relations. Motivated by nuclear collisions and ultracold atomic gases, this chapter distinguishes attractorization (the loss of sensitivity to some directions in the space of initial states) from hydrodynamization (the onset of validity of hydrodynamic constitutive relations). Using mainly conformal, boost-invariant Bjorken flow, we compare Müller-Israel-Stewart-type theories, kinetic theory, holography, and classical Yang-Mills fields. Forward attraction, produced by the decay of non-hydrodynamic modes, is distinguished from pullback attraction, which can select a unique regular solution, and from expansion-driven attraction, which can suppress initial-state sensitivity before microscopic relaxation, with or without a subsequent fluid regime. Divergent gradient expansions and their transseries completions, the state-space picture, and adiabatic hydrodynamization provide complementary descriptions. Applications to nuclear collisions include particle production, transverse energy and flow, the initialization of and linear response around attracting backgrounds, jet quenching, and attractor-informed modifications of hydrodynamic models. For ultracold Fermi gases, we review theoretical proposals for bulk-channel attractors under scattering-length drives and distinguish them from recent measurements of short-time contact and momentum-distribution dynamics.
summary: This work explores the concept of hydrodynamic attractors, which describe how complex, non-equilibrium systems approach a simple, low-dimensional late-time behavior. It rigorously distinguishes this 'attractorization' from the 'hydrodynamization' process, comparing results from nuclear collisions and ultracold atomic gases. The findings provide a unified theoretical framework for understanding how fluid dynamics emerge from microscopic interactions.
main_problem: The paper aims to distinguish between 'attractorization' (loss of initial state sensitivity) and 'hydrodynamization' (onset of hydrodynamic validity) in non-equilibrium systems.
main_result: Hydrodynamic attractors are effective low-dimensional structures that govern late-time evolution, and this concept extends constitutive relations beyond local thermal equilibrium.
method: The authors compare multiple theoretical frameworks—including kinetic theory, holography, and Israel-Stewart-type theories—using conformal, boost-invariant Bjorken flow as the primary setting.
model_or_system: The study applies to high-energy nuclear collisions (QGP) and ultracold atomic gases, utilizing theoretical tools like divergent gradient expansions and transseries completions.
key_observables: Particle production, transverse energy, flow observables, shear/bulk viscosity, and the evolution of the stress-energy tensor.
important_parameters: Proper time ($	au$), temperature ($T$), and dimensionless parameters related to viscosity ($\eta/s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on the conformal, boost-invariant Bjorken flow approximation, and it distinguishes between attractorization and hydrodynamization.
paper_structure: The paper is structured by comparing different theoretical approaches (MIS, kinetic theory, holography) to understand the transition from far-from-equilibrium dynamics to hydrodynamic behavior, detailing different types of attraction.
why_interesting: The explicit inclusion and comparison with ultracold Fermi gases provides a direct theoretical link between high-energy heavy-ion physics and controllable AMO systems.

The red curve is the stable regular solution A⋆(w) selected by the pullback limit, while the dashed magenta and the green dotted curves are approximations to the attractor given by the hydrodynamic gradient expansion truncated at first and second order respectively. The values of the parameters in the model have been chosen to match those of N = 4 SUSY YM theory in the holographic limit. Adapted from Ref. [25].

Fig. 3 shows the evolution of this attractor curve for several different dynamical descriptions. As it turns out, the differences between different descriptions are not too large, with C∞ ranging between 0.87 and 1.06.

Figure 4. Three snapshots of the evolution of an ensemble of initial states in conformal MIS theory, adapted from Ref. [33]. The red curve is the section M⋆(τ) of the attracting hypersurface on the corresponding constant-τ slice. The colored ensembles illustrate local dimensional reduction: they first become narrow, effectively one-dimensional clouds, subsequently approach the attracting section, and finally evolve along it. The background color represents the magnitude of the state-space velocity, with bluer regions corresponding to slower evolution. The plots use Cη = 0.75 and Cτπ = 1.
